text: We analyzed 3,518 job postings. The skills employers mention most aren't always the tools you'd expect. We looked at 3,518 open job postings across 81 companies' public Greenhouse boards, covering seven job categories. The goal was simple: find out which keywords employers actually use. A few findings stood out. * **Software engineering:** Mentoring appeared in nearly half of the postings, more often than Kubernetes or React. Python was the most frequently mentioned programming language. * **Product management:** More than 85% mentioned roadmaps. Jira appeared in just 7 of 421 postings. * **Marketing:** Google Ads showed up in only 6 of 347 postings, while pipeline appeared in more than half. We also noticed a pattern across roles: employers often described the practice rather than naming a specific tool. Observability came up where you might expect Grafana, and SIEM where you might expect Splunk. **What does this mean for your resume?** If you're listing tools but leaving out the responsibilities, practices, and skills explicitly mentioned in the job description, you could be missing relevant keywords. That doesn't mean stuffing your resume with buzzwords. It means describing your actual experience using language that matches the role you're applying for. One important caveat: the sample leans heavily toward tech companies and uses a single ATS platform, so these results aren't representative of every employer. The full study, including findings for sales, cybersecurity, DevOps, and accounting, is here: [https://www.zoevera.com/resume/ats-resume-keyword-study](https://www.zoevera.com/resume/ats-resume-keyword-study)

text: And... scaling productivity while minimizing human attention is precisely the frontier the AI labs are working at right now. It's a metric we track and optimize towards. So, yeah... one person with AI being more productive than 10 without is already here. Now, we're working on 1 more productive than 50 (vertical scale) AND larger teams with fleets being more productive than individuals with fleets. The question isn't, in the short term, whether one person with AI will be as productive as 100 without. It is what will organizations do with this additional capacity -- either grow into more spaces (while educating a new generation of workers) or decrease workers. Companies like Microsoft are leaning into the latter right now, but will likely reverse course or be disrupted by others that are willing to expand their company scope. AI will disrupt organizational dynamics like this. What we think of as a "company" today will seem antiquated a decade from now. Either a few companies will do everything or we'll have a Cambrian explosion of new companies or we'll evolve into more dynamic structures like SPACS -- and they'll be run by some of the worforce Microsoft is reducing today, by reskilled workers in other companies, and by graduates of new programs.
